sentences.text: This giant dinosaur possessed an unusually long neck, with the largest species measuring about 9 meters in length, supported by a neck of seventeen vertebrae.
Its head featured a wedge-shaped skull containing roughly sixty chisel-like teeth designed for stripping vegetation.
Unlike many other sauropods, the nostrils of this animal were positioned near the very tip of its snout.
The largest known species, O. tianfuensis, grew to lengths between 18 and 20.2 meters and weighed between 8.5 and 9.8 metric tons.
A specimen from Dashanpu revealed that O. tianfuensis possessed a tail club formed by modified caudal vertebrae.
In contrast, O. fuxiensis was the smallest species in the genus, reaching a length of only about 11 meters.
The name Omeisaurus comes from Mount Emei in Sichuan Province, China, where fossils were found in the lower Shaximiao Formation.
The species was described by Yang Zhongjian, known as Chung Chien Young in the West, after the first fossils were collected in 1936 by him and Charles Lewis Camp.
Unfortunately, the original skeleton of the type species O. junghsiensis was lost during World War II.
Most Omeisaurus skeletons were found between the years 1970 and 1980 during the construction of the Wujiaba Dam in Zigong.
A nearly complete skeleton found at Dashanpu was designated the holotype for O. tianfuensis and described in 1984.
Large herds of Omeisaurus likely roamed alongside stegosaurs like Tuojiangosaurus and Chungkingosaurus, making it one of the most common sauropods in Jurassic China.
Omeisaurus inhabited dense forests, and different species sometimes shared the same habitats.
A 2026 study by Kubo et al. found no evidence of significant differences in tooth microwear texture in an Omeisaurus maoianus specimen based on tooth position.
Omeisaurus was formerly classified in Euhelopodidae but is now placed in the family Mamenchisauridae, a more basal sauropod group.
A 2021 study by John D'Angelo validated most Omeisaurus species as members of the same genus, excluding O. maoianus.
Omeisaurus belongs to the class Saurischia.
Omeisaurus lived during the Middle to Late Jurassic Period (Bathonian to Oxfordian stages) in what is now China.
Omeisaurus lived from the Aalenian to the Tithonian stages, between 174.7 and 143.1 million years ago.
It is debated whether the tail club found in the same fossil beds as Omeisaurus actually belongs to Omeisaurus or to a large Shunosaurus.
The classification of O. maoianus is debated, with some analyses suggesting it is more closely related to Mamenchisaurus and Xinjiangtitan than to other Omeisaurus species.

It is debated regarding the phylogenetic relationships of Omeisaurus species, with Xing et al. (2015) and Ren et al. (2018) suggesting O. maoianus is more closely related to Mamenchisaurus than to O. tianfuensis.
